terms.definition: A direct minority equity investment by an LP into a single portfolio company, made alongside a GP's fund but outside the main fund vehicle, usually fee-light or fee-free.
An investor that commits capital to a fund (pension fund, endowment, sovereign wealth fund, insurer, family office, fund-of-funds). Has limited liability and no management role.
The manager that raises and runs the fund, sources and controls deals, and earns management fees and carried interest.
A commitment of capital to a blind-pool fund, drawn down and invested by the GP over time. The LP backs the manager, not named assets.
A fund whose specific investments are unknown at the time of commitment; the LP backs the manager's strategy and judgment rather than named assets.
A single-asset entity (LP or LLC) created to hold one co-investment. Capital is typically called and deployed almost immediately.
Co-investment offered after the GP has signed or closed the deal (post-signing). Execution is de-risked but access tends to be more competitive and returns tend to be lower than pre-signing deals.

Co-investment offered while the GP is still competing for the asset (pre-signing). Diligence is shared in real time, timelines are fastest, and there is no certainty the GP wins. Historically associated with higher gross returns (~2.7x) than post-signing (~2.2x).

The risk that the deals a GP shares with co-investors are systematically worse than the deals it keeps for the fund alone, because the GP knows more and chooses what to offer. Also called the winner's curse in this context.
In co-investment, the risk that being selected to co-invest on a deal is a negative signal — the GP is offering the deals it is least confident about, while keeping the best for the fund.

The GP's stated investment profile in terms of company size, sector, geography, and deal type. A co-investment deal outside the GP's strike zone is a red flag, as the GP may lack the expertise to generate returns.
Annual fee (commonly ~2%) on committed or invested capital; paid regardless of performance and reduces the capital actually deployed into deals.
The GP's share of profits above the hurdle rate, commonly 20%. A drag on upside that co-investors typically avoid on no-carry co-investments.
Shorthand for a standard fund fee structure: 2% annual management fee plus 20% carried interest on profits above the hurdle rate.
The minimum LP return (commonly ~8% per year) that must be achieved before the GP earns any carried interest.

A tranche in the distribution waterfall, triggered after the preferred return is paid to LPs, during which all or most proceeds flow to the GP until it has received its full carry share of profits. With 100% catch-up and 20% carry: catch-up amount = 0.25 × preferred return.
The contractual order in which fund proceeds are split between LPs and GP: return of capital → preferred return → GP catch-up → carried interest split.
Multiple on Invested Capital. Total value (distributions + residual NAV) divided by invested capital. The primary return metric for a single investment.
Total Value to Paid-In. (Distributions + residual NAV) divided by paid-in capital. Equals DPI + RVPI. The primary return multiple for a fund.
Distributions to Paid-In. Realized cash returned to LPs divided by paid-in capital. Measures what has actually been returned in cash.
Residual Value to Paid-In. Unrealized NAV divided by paid-in capital. Measures the paper value not yet distributed.
Internal Rate of Return. The discount rate that sets the net present value of all cash flows (contributions and distributions) to zero. Time-sensitive; affected by the timing of cash flows.

The early-life dip in a fund's net return/NAV, caused by management fee payments and capital deployed into companies that have not yet appreciated or been realized. Returns later curve upward — creating a J shape over time.

A performance comparison method that replicates PE cash flows in a public index investment of the same timing. Kaplan-Schoar PME (KS-PME) > 1 means PE outperformed the index. Used in academic co-investment research (FIL, BJS).

A decomposition of a co-investment's projected equity return into its four components: EBITDA growth, margin expansion, multiple change (re-rating), and debt paydown (deleveraging). A thesis leaning on multiple expansion is fragile; one driven by EBITDA growth and deleveraging is sturdier.

On equal footing. In co-investment, this means the co-investor holds the same security, entry price, and terms as the GP's fund. Any structural difference (worse pricing, subordinated instrument) is a red flag.
A contractual right allowing the GP to compel co-investors to sell their stake alongside the fund in an exit, preventing minority co-investors from blocking a deal.
A contractual right allowing co-investors to sell their stake alongside the GP on the same terms when the GP exits, protecting minority investors from being left behind.
The year a fund or deal begins investing. Diversifying co-investments across vintage years reduces correlation and timing risk, as different vintages are exposed to different market cycles.
Committed but uninvested capital in a fund. High industry dry powder levels can indicate competitive deal markets and elevated entry multiples.

The return advantage a co-investor has over a fund LP on the same underlying deal, equal to the fund gross MOIC minus the fund net MOIC. This cushion (roughly 12–24% of gross MOIC under 2-and-20) is how much a co-investment can underperform on a gross basis and still match the fund net.

The maximum percentage of a fund's total commitments that can be invested in a single portfolio company, typically 10–20% per fund LPA. GPs use co-investment to execute large deals without breaching this limit.

Adjustments that increase reported EBITDA by adding back one-time, non-recurring, or non-cash items. Aggressive add-backs inflate apparent EBITDA, reduce apparent leverage, and flatter entry valuations. A common source of underwriting risk in co-investments.
EBITDA divided by interest expense. A measure of a company's ability to service its debt from operating cash flow. A key covenant metric and stress-test variable in leveraged co-investments.

Institutional Limited Partners Association. Industry body that publishes principles and best practices for private equity investing, including guidance on co-investment transparency, fee alignment, and the allocation of co-investment opportunities.
The body within an LP organization that formally approves or rejects an investment. In co-investment, the compressed timeline requires a standing IC or delegated authority that can convene quickly.
The governing contract of a private equity fund, setting out the rights and obligations of the LP and GP, including concentration limits, investment period, fee terms, and distribution waterfall.
